subject: Your comments on a heavily parameterized model

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Your comments on a heavily parameterized model
parts:
Hi, I attach a stan model script for a framework with multiple outcome types, all of which share (disjoint dimensions of) multivariate random effects.   I've successfully run this framework in JAGS, but wanted to employ more flexible covariance matrix priors and also compare runtimes under stan.   My stan model crashes R after a 5 or so minutes of running, post-compilation and linking (from rstan 1.0.2).   R crashes generally happen for me when running C++ code written under Rcpp if I hit a numerical singularity.    This model, though simpler, is of a similar flavor of a previous model I was unable to successfully run in stan.   Both models are relatively heavily parameterized (though well-powered under the data).   I thought the attached model might work because the script generally hugs the shore of what I see successfully employed on the user list, with nothing fancy.   I've tried alternative prior formulations of relatively greater informativeness, but with the same result of crashing R.   I would appreciate your quick scan of the script to see if I have made some obviously poor construction choices.   Otherwise, I tend to think that the model is too richly parameterized for massive joint updating in a metropolis fashion.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Your comments on a heavily parameterized model
parts:
We shouldn't be crashing R ever, although it happens. When it does, please follow the procedure for a runtime error

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/FXHj6fn0SC0J

I didn't see anything wrong with this model, but it is hard to tell with a long .stan file. I also doubt that the multidimensionality is a major problem, per se. I think Marcus has done models with 50,000 parameters in Stan. He and Bob got your previous model to work (sort of) by overriding the defaults Stan uses for adapting. Yesterday, Matt found and fixed a bug with how the sampling was starting. And Bob has put in some more checks to prevent mysterious crashes. Both of those will be in the next release of Stan and rstan.

One thing, which is presumably unrelated to anything but execution speed:

        /* priors on by-level correlation matrices */
        R_t     ~ lkj_corr(eta);
        R_s     ~ lkj_corr(eta);
        R_v     ~ lkj_corr(eta);
        R_r     ~ lkj_corr(eta);

Don't bother explicitly coding uniform priors on parameters (except if the parameter is a bound for another parameter). The above entails 4 checks that the correlation matrices don't have an NaNs, four checks of symmetry, four checks that the diagonals are all 1.0, and four Cholesky decompositions to determine that they are positive definite (all of which should hold by construction) for every leapfrog step of every iteration, even though the uniform priors do not change the posterior distribution. Only go through all that if eta != 1.0.

Ben
